meta.title: Who really said "Nothing is ugly as long as it is alive"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Coco Chanel really said it. Her biographer Marcel Haedrich recorded the line in Coco Chanel secrète (1971); the English wording is a 1972 translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nothing is ugly as long as it is alive'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: the line comes from Marcel Haedrich's 1971 Chanel biography — 'Rien n'est laid, du moment que c'est vivant.' The English wording dates from 1972.

answer.label: Spoken by

answer.sourceLine: Chanel said it, and there is a book to point at: her biographer Marcel Haedrich recorded the remark in Coco Chanel secrète (Paris: Robert Laffont, 1971) as “Rien n’est laid, du moment que c’est vivant.” The familiar English wording is Charles Lam Markmann’s translation, published in 1972 as Coco Chanel: Her Life, Her Secrets, where Quote Investigator verified it on paper ↗ at pages 253–54.

source.excerpt: Nothing is ugly as long as it is alive.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the line to Marcel Haedrich, printing the French original from Coco Chanel secrète (1971), page 307, and the English from Markmann’s 1972 translation at pages 253–54 — marked verified with scans and verified on paper respectively — and concludes that Chanel deserves credit on her biographer’s testimony.
Wikiquote ↗ also lists the line among Chanel’s sourced quotes, attributing it to Haedrich’s Coco Chanel: Her Life, Her Secrets, though it dates that English title to 1971.

The Open Library edition record ↗ settles the chain independently of Quote Investigator: the translation was originally published Boston: Little, Brown, 1972, and is a translation of Coco Chanel secrète, Paris: Laffont, 1971.

The Internet Archive holds scans of both printings — the Little, Brown edition ↗ and a London Hale printing ↗ that names Charles Lam Markmann as translator. Pagination differs between them, so the 253–54 reference belongs to the Little, Brown text.
source.excerptNote: In Haedrich’s book the sentence opens a short passage rather than standing alone: Chanel goes on to answer women who complain to her about having rather thick legs by asking whether those legs carry them, which is what she says matters. The French original of the line reads “Rien n’est laid, du moment que c’est vivant.” The full passage is transcribed in both languages by Quote Investigator ↗; it is quoted only in part here because the book remains in copyright.

author.name: Coco Chanel
author.heading: About Coco Chanel
author.metaLine: 1883–1971 · French couturier, founder of the House of Chanel
author.bio: Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel was born in Saumur in 1883 and died in Paris in January 1971. She built the House of Chanel on clothes that let a body move — jersey promoted from underwear to couture, corseting and stiffening thrown out, real pockets, necklines you could breathe in — alongside the little black dress and Chanel No. 5. After roughly fifteen years away from fashion she reopened her house in 1954, and the collections of that comeback are the ones that fixed the Chanel look for good.

misattribution.heading: What gets mangled
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a Coco Chanel quotation, the credit here is not the problem — no rival claimant has surfaced, and the specialists land on Chanel. What travels badly is the citation attached to it, and the context it gets torn out of.

items.who: Wikiquote and the aggregators downstream of it
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ cites the line to “Coco Chanel : Her Life, Her Secrets (1971)” — but that English title did not exist in 1971. The edition record ↗ is explicit: the translation was first published in Boston by Little, Brown in 1972, from Coco Chanel secrète, Paris: Laffont, 1971. The year belongs to the French book, the title to the English one.

The sentence comes to us through two hands that are not Chanel’s: her biographer wrote it down in a section headed “Elle disait” — she said — and Charles Lam Markmann turned it into English. There is no letter, manuscript or recording in Chanel’s own hand behind the exact nine words, only Haedrich’s testimony ↗, which is what Quote Investigator rests the credit on.

Presented alone it reads as a soft line about beauty in general. In the book it is the opening of a pointed exchange in which Chanel answers women picking at their own thick legs by asking whether the legs carry them — a remark about bodies that work, not about aesthetics (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution holds: Quote Investigator concludes that Chanel deserves credit ↗ on her biographer’s testimony. Cite it as Haedrich, Coco Chanel secrète (1971) — and note that the English you are quoting is Markmann’s, 1972.

context.heading: Why she said it
lead: Chanel’s whole design programme was an argument about bodies that work. She took jersey out of underwear and put it into couture, dropped the corseting and the stiffening, and cut clothes you could climb stairs in — the point being freedom of movement for women who had somewhere to be (Wikipedia ↗). The remark belongs to that programme. It is not a compliment paid to beauty; it is a refusal to rank bodies at all.

In Haedrich’s book the line is not a standalone slogan either. It opens a short exchange in which Chanel answers women who complain to her about their thick legs by asking whether those legs carry them — the whole thrust being that a body that does its job is not a flawed ornament (Quote Investigator ↗).
context.detailsSummary: How the sentence travelled into English
detailsBody: The French original appeared in 1971 in Coco Chanel secrète, in chapter 21 (“Coco au travail”), in a section headed “Elle disait” — “She said” — which is exactly what it is: a gathering of remarks Haedrich had from her, not a manuscript she wrote.

The English wording most people know dates from the following year. Markmann’s translation was published in Boston by Little, Brown in 1972, with the passage in the corresponding “She Said” section of chapter 21. Quote Investigator also documents a May 1972 Vogue feature under Haedrich’s byline that carried the quotation and pushed it into wider circulation, and a 1977 entry in Elaine Partnow’s The Quotable Woman: 1800–1975 that cites Haedrich’s book by name.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces "Nothing is ugly as long as it is alive" to Marcel Haedrich's Coco Chanel secrète (1971, Robert Laffont, ch. 21 "Coco au travail", section "Elle disait", p. 307), gives the French original "Rien n'est laid, du moment que c'est vivant", cites the 1972 Charles Lam Markmann translation Coco Chanel: Her Life, Her Secrets (Little, Brown, Boston) at pp. 253-254, notes a 1 May 1972 Vogue feature under Haedrich's byline and a 1977 entry in Elaine Partnow's The Quotable Woman: 1800-1975, and concludes that Coco Chanel deserves credit based on her biographer's testimony.

Wikiquote lists "Nothing is ugly as long as it is alive" among Coco Chanel's quotes with the source "As quoted in Coco Chanel : Her Life, Her Secrets (1971) by Marcel Haedrich", and has no Misattributed or Disputed section covering it.
The Open Library edition record states the translation was originally published Boston: Little, Brown, 1972, and is a translation of Coco Chanel secrète, Paris: Laffont, 1971.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of Coco Chanel; Her Life, Her Secrets by Marcel Haedrich, published by Little Brown and Co in 1972.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of Coco Chanel, her life, her secrets by Marcel Haedrich, translated by Charles Lam Markmann, published by Hale, London, 1972, 277 pages plus 16 pages of plates.

Coco Chanel was born Gabrielle Bonheur Chanel on 19 August 1883 in Saumur and died 10 January 1971 in Paris; she founded the House of Chanel, brought jersey into couture, introduced the little black dress and Chanel No. 5, rejected corseting in favour of clothes allowing free movement, and revived her fashion house in 1954 after about fifteen years away.
Marcel Haedrich (1913-2003) directed the editorial board of Marie Claire when the magazine resumed publication in 1954, for ten years, and wrote Coco Chanel secrète (1971).
